title: Change planning under platform and regional constraints

opening.headline: We explore how to convert a change constrained by support schedule, platform, and region limitations into a phased plan with a clear sequence through constraint decomposition.
body: Let's consider the scenario where we need to upgrade the operating cluster without interrupting AI inference services. Currently, Kubernetes minor versions are approaching end-of-support, AI compatibility certification is tied to version-specific checklists for Kubernetes, and inference processing must occur only within allowed regions. Considering all three aspects together makes it difficult to determine where to begin.

In this lesson, we learn how to categorize constraints by type—such as time, platform, and region—and present them in a table, showing how much each constraint can flex. We then filter candidate plans against these constraints, examine the principles of reducing risk through backups, staged application, and rollback points, and finally examine a case study of a plan that maintains regional constraints as support ends.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: The given constraints can be decomposed by time, platform, and region.
It is possible to determine whether the change plan satisfies constraints.

screens.title: A change subject to three constraints simultaneously
screens.lead: Please review the scene in the figure where three constraints overlap in a single change. Proceed by considering for yourself which constraint should be addressed first.

visual.alt: A timeline, platform, and region constraints overlaid on a single change request diagram.
labels: Change Request: Cluster Upgrade + Inference Service Maintenance
Platform Constraints (AI Compatibility Checklists by Kubernetes Version)
Region constraints (processing allowed only within regions that are permitted)

paragraphs: A change request has been submitted. The operational cluster should be upgraded, but the AI inference service must continue to be provided. At first glance, this may seem like a simple request, but it is constrained in three distinct directions.

First, there are version constraints. Current Kubernetes minor versions have predefined end-of-support dates, after which no security updates or bug fixes are provided. Second, there are platform constraints. AI compatibility certification is tied to version-specific checklists for Kubernetes, and removed API versions are no longer available starting from a given release. Third, there are region constraints. Inference processing must occur only within allowed regions, and narrowing the region scope reduces the number of available models.
Looking at these three aspects as a single unit makes it unclear where to begin. However, when breaking them down individually, a clear order begins to emerge.

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: Among these three, what are the one with a fixed date, the one with a defined rule, and the one that can be chosen? This distinction is used throughout the class.

screens.outro: First, let's recall our experience with planned similar changes.

screens.title: Have you ever planned a change involving conflicting constraints?
screens.lead: When you select a question, the instructor's thoughts are revealed. Since you're not submitting or entering anything, first recall your own experience and then try it.

items.prompt: What was determined first at that time?
items.answer: Many teams start with obvious milestones. However, the first thing to establish is the immutable constraints. Use non-negotiable elements such as dates and regulations as a baseline, and position the rest around them, so the plan remains stable.

items.prompt: Was there a point from which we could revert?
items.answer: A plan designed to be completed in one go has no fallback point if problems arise midway. By establishing clear checkpoints between stages in advance, failure impacts are limited to just one stage.

items.prompt: What was the most restrictive constraint?
items.answer: The most restrictive constraint is typically the one that arrives earliest and prevents any movement. It determines the start time and sequence of the plan. In this class, we use a constraint table as a tool to illustrate this concept.

screens.outro: Then let's look at how to present constraints in a table.

screens.title: Constraint breakdown: List three constraints in the table
screens.lead: Check in the table how each constraint is organized with its source, content, and the degree of flexibility. The column in the last column is the key that identifies the most restrictive constraint.

visual.alt: A diagram placed along the axis from being unable to move constraints to being negotiable.

data.caption: Decomposition of Constraints Affected by Changes
rows: Each minor release has a defined end-of-support date, after which it no longer receives security updates or bug fixes.
Upgrading by skipping minor versions is not supported; the number of stages to upgrade equals the required time.
Unmovable: The step cannot be reduced.
Removed API versions are no longer provided starting from that release, so the old apiVersion manifest must be migrated before the upgrade.
AI suitability certification is available by version checklist (v1.35, v1.36, v1.37) and is valid for one year per product and configuration unit.
Some negotiation possible: you can choose which version to target.
Cross-region configuration ranges from global to home region-only, and the more strict the setting, the fewer models are available.
Negotiations are possible only within the scope defined by residency requirements.
data.notes: When filling out a table, it is important to indicate the source for each row. Having a source allows others to verify whether a constraint is truly infeasible. When multiple constraints exist, the one that arises first is typically the most restrictive, and this determines the start time and sequence of the plan.

screens.outro: We have created the constraint table, so now let's compare the candidate plan against this table.

screens.title: Select a feasible plan: compare candidates against constraints
screens.lead: Select each candidate plan one by one using the tap function and compare it against the rows of the constraint table. The objective is to verify which candidate is rejected in which row.

tabs.label: Option 1: Upload once
tabs.body: We plan to upgrade the cluster to the latest minor version in one go. It appears to be the fastest option. However, skipping a minor version during an upgrade is not supported, so this candidate is blocked by the "Not Movable" row in the constraints table. Therefore, this candidate is immediately disqualified during the control phase. The fastest plan is not the best option.

tabs.label: Option 2: Gradual + Region Retention
tabs.body: Promote minors one step at a time, while keeping the current scope unchanged for region settings. Time constraints are satisfied once a sufficient number of steps' time is available, and platform constraints are satisfied by first moving the manifest and then comparing it against the checklist of the target version. Since region constraints maintain the existing scope, they are not violated. This candidate satisfies all three constraints.

tabs.label: Option 3: Gradual + Regional Expansion
tabs.body: We plan to gradually increase our scale while expanding the region scope to enable more models. We have satisfied the scheduling and platform constraints. However, expanding the region scope will increase the number of models, but may result in processing occurring outside the allowed regions, thereby violating residency requirements. Additionally, when upgrades and region changes are combined into a single change, it becomes difficult to determine the root cause of issues.

tabs.label: Selection criteria
tabs.body: Decisions are made based on a matrix, not intuition. Each candidate is evaluated against the rows of the constraint matrix to indicate whether their constraints are satisfied. Candidates who fail to meet the constraints are eliminated first. If multiple candidates satisfy the constraints, the one that is easier to revert is selected. In this case, two candidates remain, and if regional expansion is truly necessary, they are separated into a distinct case for individual review. This approach enables clear justification to others for why this plan was chosen, why other candidates were eliminated due to specific constraints, and precisely which row should be re-examined if the plan needs to change.

screens.outro: We will examine methods for reducing risks to ensure that the plan succeeds.

screens.title: The principle of risk mitigation and rollback points
screens.lead: The following is an example of a balanced plan reorganized into a change plan document. Select each highlighted section one at a time to verify which risks each part mitigates.

data.text:
Upgrade Plan: Upgrade from Operating Cluster 1.34 to 1.36 (Assumed)

[Prerequisite] The processing location is permitted only within the EU. The region setting is not changed by this update.  
[Preparation] Compare the removal API table with the manifest and first migrate the apiVersion to the new version.  
[First Upgrade] Rollback point A: After completing the backup, increment from 1.34 to 1.35. Deploy the control plane first, then the worker nodes.  
[Second Upgrade] Rollback point B: Upgrade from 1.35 to 1.36 after confirming that the 1.35 state is stable.  
[Post-verification] Cross-check against the AI compatibility checklist and documentation for the version, ensuring validity, and re-verify the processing location via lookup.  
[Separation] Expansion or contraction of the region scope is addressed as a separate change from this plan.

marks.span: The processing location is permitted only within the EU. The region setting is not changed by this update.
marks.note: The principle stated at the beginning of the plan is that only one constraint should be changed at a time. By fixing the region setting, it becomes certain that issues during upgrades are not due to region changes, thus making root cause analysis easier.

marks.span: Compare the removal API table with the manifest and first migrate the apiVersion to the new version.
marks.note: When migrating to the new API, default values may change. For example, the default value of webhook `failurePolicy` changes from `Ignore` to `Fail`. By comparing these values in advance, rather than on the day of upgrade, you can prevent deployment failures.

marks.span: Rollback point A: After completing the backup, increment from 1.34 to 1.35.
marks.note: The rollback point is placed between stages. `kubeadm upgrade` does not interfere with the workload, but backing up application-level state is a best practice. If issues arise, you can pause at this point and make a decision.

marks.span: Deploy the control plane first, then the worker nodes.
marks.note: Sequential application reduces the scope of impact. It divides the nodes into first the control plane node, then the remaining control plane nodes, and finally the worker nodes, applying changes one at a time so that not all parts are modified simultaneously.

marks.span: Expansion or contraction of the region scope is addressed as a separate change from this plan.
marks.note: Mixing upgrades and region changes makes it difficult to determine which one caused an issue and complicates rollback processes. Separating them into independent changes allows each to have its own rollback point.

screens.outro: Now we will walk through a case approaching end-of-support from start to finish.

screens.title: Explanation: Plan to maintain region constraints as support end-of-life approaches
screens.lead: The instructor explains a case step by step. Select the right arrow to proceed to the next step.

visual.alt: Preparation, pre-verification, two-stage incremental upgrades, post-verification, following a planned sequence that includes rollback points.

steps.title: situation
steps.body: The cluster is operating in a minor version that has limited headroom until end-of-support and is two levels behind the currently supported version. Inference processing for this service is permitted only within the EU. Schedules remain fixed, regions can only move within the specified range, and the platform follows the checklist and API removal list of the target version.

steps.title: Step 1: Preprocessing
steps.body: Before upgrading, compare the release notes and removal API tables. During a two-step upgrade, all removals from releases in between are targeted. First, migrate your manifest from the old apiVersion to the new version, then review items whose defaults have changed in the new version. This ensures that the deployment does not break on the day of upgrade.

steps.title: Step 2: Pre-verification
steps.body: The region setting is not being modified in this change. Additionally, we verify whether the current processing location falls within the EU scope by checking the configuration and record this information. By recording this, we can later repeat the same query after the change to verify whether the setting remains unchanged.

steps.title: Step 3: Gradual Upgrade
steps.body: Since we cannot skip minor versions, we proceed step by step. At each step, we proceed in order: first the control plane node, then the remaining control plane nodes, and finally the worker nodes. When upgrading the minor kubelet, we first drain the node and schedule the time accordingly, considering that all containers will be restarted after the upgrade.

steps.title: Step 4: Rollback Point
steps.body: Backup the app-level state before raising each minor issue, and predefine criteria for when to proceed to the next step and when to stop. If a problem occurs, halt at that point to investigate the cause. Since only one constraint is changed at a time, the number of potential causes is limited.

steps.title: Step 5: Post-verification
steps.body: Once the target version is reached, the AI suitability checklist and evidence for that version are cross-checked to ensure they remain valid. Certification is tied to the product and its components, and specific to the Kubernetes version, so it is important that the platform provider holds certification for the target version. The processing location is also verified again using the same query and is compared against prior records.

steps.title: result
steps.body: The schedule is kept, and the region and platform constraints are maintained without change. This result was achieved because we systematically broke down the three constraints one by one and established their order.

screens.outro: I will summarize the reasoning order used in the case at the end.

screens.title: Breaking down the constraints reveals the order.
screens.lead: This course covers constraint decomposition, candidate controls, and risk mitigation as a single procedure.

paragraphs: Constraints affected by changes are first divided by schedule, platform, and region. By indicating whether each constraint is immovable or negotiable alongside its rationale, the most restrictive constraint becomes evident, thereby determining the start time and sequence of the plan.

Next, compare the candidate plans against the constraint table rows. Eliminate candidates that do not satisfy the constraints, and when multiple candidates are feasible, prefer those that are easier to revert. The intuitive belief that the fastest plan is best collapses when confronted with the constraint that it cannot skip minor issues.

Finally, it reduces risk by performing backups, applying changes sequentially from the control plane, pre-comparing default value changes in the new API, and separating upgrades from region changes into distinct change sets. The principle is to move only one constraint at a time and to establish rollback points between stages.

Going back to the initial scene, the reason we felt overwhelmed by the three constraints simultaneously was that they appeared as a single, unified group. When broken down into a constraints table, they become a sequence of ordered tasks. This approach can be used unchanged even if the types of constraints differ.

callout.label: organizing
callout.text: Breaking down the constraints reveals the order.

glossary.def: This involves categorizing and dividing constraints by source, such as specific instances, platforms, and regions, and presenting them in a table along with the extent to which they are movable.
After filtering out invalid candidates, this is the execution order arranged in stages according to dependency relationships.
Measures to reduce the likelihood of failure and the scope of impact, such as backup, staged deployment, and pre-comparison.
These are pre-defined stage boundaries at which the process halts or rolls back when issues occur.

misconceptions.myth: The fastest plan to reach the latest version is the best approach.
misconceptions.fact: Upgrading over a minor version is not supported, so the number of stages directly corresponds to the required time. A rapid plan may fail due to constraints.

misconceptions.myth: All constraints have the same weight.
misconceptions.fact: There are constraints that are fixed and unchangeable, like an end-of-support date, and there are negotiable constraints, like a target version or configuration value. Distinguishing between them provides clarity in order.

misconceptions.myth: Upgrading and region changes can be efficient when performed together.
misconceptions.fact: It is difficult to determine the cause of an issue and to roll back when multiple constraints are moved at once. It is safer to move one constraint at a time.

closing.lead: Summarizes the key points of this class.
points: Breaking down the constraints reveals the order.
Each schedule, platform, and region is listed in the table together with its basis and degree of flexibility.
Eliminate and revert candidates that do not meet the requirements, and select a plan that is easy to reverse.
Move only one constraint at a time and establish rollback points between steps.
